findings.title: Options-object pLimit unexpectedly rejects cleared tasks by default
findings.cause: The options-object destructuring changed the implicit rejectOnClear default from false to true at index.js:7, while the documented and typed option default remains false.
findings.impact: Callers using pLimit({concurrency: 1}) and clearing teardown queues now get AbortError rejections from every pending task. This breaks the documented default and can turn previously quiet shutdown/discard paths into unhandled rejections or failed Promise.all chains.
findings.evidence: index.js:7 destructures {concurrency, rejectOnClear = true}; index.js:79-88 rejects queued entries when rejectOnClear is true. readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106 state rejectOnClear is boolean with Default: false.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1}); const running = limit(() => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 30))); const pending = limit(() => 'never'); await Promise.resolve(); limit.clearQueue(); try { await pending; console.log('pending resolved'); } catch (error) { console.log(error.name); } await running;" prints AbortError.

findings.title: Falsy non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass validation
findings.cause: The validation guard at index.js:12 only checks the type when rejectOnClear is truthy, so values like 0, empty string, or null are accepted even though the public option is boolean.
findings.impact: Invalid configuration is silently accepted and coerced into clearQueue behavior instead of failing fast. This weakens the runtime contract and can hide caller mistakes that TypeScript would reject.
findings.evidence: index.js:12 uses `if (rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean')`; index.d.ts:106 declares `readonly rejectOnClear?: boolean`; readme.md:46-49 documents Type: boolean.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; try { pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: 0}); console.log('accepted'); } catch (error) { console.log(error.name + ': ' + error.message); }" prints accepted.

findings.title: limit.map omits mapper indexes for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The map implementation now passes the index only when Array.isArray(iterable) is true, using undefined for Set, iterator, and other iterable inputs at index.js:108-112.
findings.impact: The documented API says the mapper receives both item and index for any iterable. Code that maps Sets or iterator inputs and uses index for ordering, batching, labels, or offsets now receives undefined instead.
findings.evidence: index.js:108-112 computes iterableIsArray and passes `iterableIsArray ? index : undefined`; readme.md:78-85 and index.d.ts:29-43 document the mapper index and Promise.all(Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => ...)) equivalence.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit(2); console.log(JSON.stringify(await limit.map(new Set(['a','b']), (value, index) => [value, index])));" prints [["a",null],["b",null]] because JSON.stringify converts undefined array entries to null.

findings.title: limitFunction drops all caller arguments
findings.cause: limitFunction returns a zero-argument wrapper at index.js:124 and calls function_() without forwarding the wrapper's received arguments.
findings.impact: Any limited function that depends on parameters now receives undefined values. This breaks the TypeScript signature, documented helper behavior, and the repository benchmark path that calls limitedTask(delay, i).
findings.evidence: index.js:121-124 returns `() => limit(() => function_())`; index.d.ts:133-136 declares the returned function as `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`; benchmark.js:193-194 calls a limitFunction wrapper with delay and index arguments.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import {limitFunction} from './index.js'; const fn = limitFunction((x, y) => x + y, {concurrency: 1}); console.log(await fn(2, 3));" prints NaN instead of 5.

findings.title: Infinity concurrency is rejected despite prior public behavior
findings.cause: validateConcurrency at index.js:127-130 now requires Number.isInteger(concurrency), removing the explicit Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY allowance present in the repository baseline.
findings.impact: Callers using pLimit(Infinity) to disable limiting while preserving the same scheduling API now get a TypeError at construction time. This is a behavioral regression from the checked-in baseline.
findings.evidence: index.js:128 rejects any non-integer; `git show HEAD:index.js` shows the baseline condition accepted `(Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) && concurrency > 0`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; try { pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY); console.log('accepted'); } catch (error) { console.log(error.name + ': ' + error.message); }" prints TypeError: Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up.
